Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-11

Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Argus Eng Manager), Sana Malik (Argus Backend), Luis Ortega (Argus Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Quick SDK walkthrough covering Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth (API key vs SSO/token), environment setup, example code for realtime streaming, discussion of Dedicated vs Hosted for Argus workloads, and next steps to run a short perf check and share security/compliance docs.

Topics:
- Quickstart setup (pip/npm installs, env vars)
- Auth patterns (api key, service tokens, SSO/SAML integration)
- Sample code: Python sync/async, Typescript streaming SDK, server-side vs client-side usage
- Observability and logs, RBAC, audit logs, KMS for data encryption
- Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs (latency vs cost, VPC options)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood. we'll do a quick 30–40 minute walkthrough of the SDKs and then leave time for q&a. priya's going to demo some code.
[00:12] Evan: great thanks, jordan. we're mainly interested in low-latency inference for product search and some chat features. budget is tight but latency matters.
[00:22] Priya: cool, can you share what your current stack looks like? are you using k8s, serverless, what language per service?
[00:30] Evan: we run on k8s in AWS, backend mostly node/typescript and some python microservices. we have a private VPC and strict egress rules, so networking is a concern.
[00:40] Sana: also need SOC2 controls and ability to use customer managed KMS; legal will ask about data retention and audit logs.
[00:47] Jordan: totally — we support KMS integrations and have SOC2, ISO certs; i'll share the compliance pack. priya, take it away on the quickstart.
[00:55] Priya: ok jumping in. first install: pip install redwood-sdk for python, npm install @redwood-ai/sdk for typescript. set REDWOOD_API_KEY or REDWOOD_ORG_TOKEN as env vars. example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxxx. note: for private deployments you can swap endpoint to your private control plane: export REDWOOD_API_BASE=https://private.redwood.argus.local
[01:25] Evan: quick q — can we use SSO for service accounts or only API keys?
[01:30] Jordan: you can use SSO/SAML for interactive users and mint short-lived service tokens via our org auth flow; also support OIDC providers. for service-to-service we recommend scoped api keys or short-lived tokens backed by your SSO.
[01:44] Priya: showing python snippet now — sync example: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.chat.create(model='redwood-1-large', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'summarize this product description'}]); print(resp.text)
[02:05] Priya: the async pattern is similar, and we also support streaming with async iterators for real-time UI.
[02:15] Sana: any rate limit handling built in? we want graceful backpressure in our queues.
[02:20] Priya: built in retries and backoff; plus local sdk helpers for token-level batching. you can configure max_concurrency and batch windows to tune cost/latency tradeoffs.
[02:33] Luis: how do we secure keys in k8s?
[02:36] Jordan: recommend k8s secrets with your KMS or use workload identity to fetch short-lived tokens. for Dedicated/private we can integrate with your KMS directly so keys don't leave your control.
[02:50] Priya: switching to typescript quickstart — basic usage: import { Redwood } from '@redwood-ai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const stream = client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-1-small', messages: [...] }); for ( await const chunk of stream ) { // update UI }
[03:12] Evan: streaming latency looks good from the demos. how heavy is client-side bandwidth?
[03:18] Priya: streaming sends deltas; tokenization overhead is small. for large responses we recommend chunked rendering.
[03:26] Jordan: a note on endpoints: hosted api = api.redwood.ai, dedicated will be your dedicated endpoint in region, private has private base url. we can route by region for latency.
[03:40] Evan: can we pin model versions? we need reproducible outputs for audits.
[03:44] Priya: yes you can pin exact model versions and also maintain rollout policies — canary/A-B and automatic fallback to smaller models if capacity is constrained.
[03:55] Sana: what about observability? we need token-level cost and tracebacks per request.
[04:00] Priya: redwood console surfaces per-route latency, token breakouts, and trace ids you can correlate with your logs. we provide tracing hooks and a logging endpoint to forward audit logs into your SIEM.
[04:12] Luis: curious about kv cache mention in docs — is that client-side or server-side?
[04:17] Priya: that's server-side prefix/KV cache to speed up chat continuations; we also have local client caching helpers to reduce token usage for repeated prompts.
[04:27] Evan: we saw competitors pricing that seems lower for raw tokens; how do you position on cost?
[04:31] Jordan: good question — unit cost varies by model and throughput. our Optimize toolkit will recommend batching, quantization, and model variants to meet latency/cost targets. often we save customers money via smarter batching/caching compared to naive calls to managed APIs.
[04:50] Sana: security review: do you have SOC2 docs and pen test reports?
[04:54] Jordan: yes, i will send SOC2 report and our pen test summary, plus details on RBAC and SSO.
[04:59] Evan: about private deployment — how does network egress work? we have strict firewall rules and want in-region data processing.
[05:06] Priya: for Private you run the control plane in your VPC, or we provide a customer-managed package on-prem. egress can be internal only; we support VPC peering and private endpoints.
[05:17] Evan: OK good. what does the SDK do for retries and idempotency?
[05:21] Priya: SDK exposes idempotency keys at request time and automatic retry policies; we give knobs for total retries and per-call timeouts.
[05:30] Jordan: demoing a short local quickstart app now — link in chat: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart and docs at https://docs.redwood.ai/sdk-quickstart (note: example repo contains Python flask example and Next.js typescript streaming example)
[05:50] Sana: perfect, we'll try the Next.js demo. any gotchas for server-side vs client-side keys?
[05:56] Priya: never expose long-lived keys to the browser; use a server-side proxy or mint session tokens via the auth endpoint. ephemeral tokens for client streaming are supported.
[06:08] Luis: curious about Dedicated capacity sizing. our peak is 120 qps with bursts to 400 qps.
[06:14] Jordan: for that profile we'd recommend Dedicated with autoscaling and a burst policy; priya will run a quick capacity estimate and we'll follow up with cost numbers.
[06:27] Priya: note on quantization: if you want lower cost models, we can recommend int8/4 quantized variants for similar quality on many workloads; Optimize will flag quality regressions and track evals.
[06:44] Evan: we'd also like to run a small POC with a subset of users. timeline is 2–4 weeks for POC, then procurement.
[06:53] Jordan: sounds good. next steps: I'll send the quickstart links, SOC2 and security docs, and priya will run a perf smoke and share a short diff of Hosted vs Dedicated cost/latency.
[07:03] Sana: will do. also legal wants data processing addendum and support for customer-managed KMS.
[07:08] Jordan: we'll include the DPA template and KMS integration notes.
[07:14] Evan: last q on pricing model: do you do usage + reserved?
[07:18] Jordan: yes hosted api is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits and support tiers. we can show both scenarios in the follow-up deck.
[07:30] Priya: any other technical q?
[07:33] Luis: one more — offline batching for high throughput async jobs, do you have a recommended pattern?
[07:37] Priya: yes use our batch endpoint or run a worker pool that aggregates prompts and calls the batch API; supports partial responses and idempotency.
[07:48] Jordan: ok wrapping up. i'll share artifacts and we can schedule the poc kickoff once you send sample traffic.
[07:55] Evan: thanks everyone.
